item.title: Reading the Reasoning Traces Behind ARC-AGI-3
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Greg Kamradt at ARC Prize published an analysis of 160 replays and reasoning traces from OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 and Anthropic’s Opus 4.7 on ARC-AGI-3, the 135-environment benchmark that withholds instructions and forces the model to infer rules from sparse feedback. GPT-5.5 scored 0.43%, Opus 4.7 scored 0.18%.

What the article reports: three failure modes pulled from the reasoning traces.

  • True local effect, false world model. The model correctly notices that an action changes a local property (“ACTION3 rotates the object”) but doesn’t translate the observation into a rule that governs play (“orient the object to match the target before acting”). The observation is right; the world model is missing.
  • Wrong level of abstraction from training data. Models map unfamiliar mechanics onto games they’ve seen: Tetris, Frogger, Sokoban, Flood-It, Breakout. A visual resemblance becomes a full gameplay theory and action selection follows the wrong script.
  • Solved the level, didn’t learn the game. A level can be beaten with a mistaken read of the primitive (“click teleports the character” when the real mechanic is push-to-match), and the reward then cements the wrong theory for subsequent levels.

Two illustrations from the article.

The article closes with a named contrast between the two models: Opus compressed its observations into a confident wrong theory, GPT-5.5 kept the hypothesis space open but never committed to a plan. “Opus had the wrong compression, GPT-5.5 failed to compress.”

My Notes

  • The three failure modes each break a different step in observe → rule → plan → commit. Failure 1 breaks between observation and rule. Failure 2 swaps in a rule borrowed from training data instead of inferring one from evidence. Failure 3 commits to a rule the reward didn’t validate. That’s more useful than “the models can’t reason,” because it points at which step to instrument in a harness.

  • Failure 3 is the one most likely to show up outside ARC-AGI-3. It’s the empirical version of the metacognitive-evaluation gap: if the agent can’t ask why it won the last level, outcome reward reinforces whatever theory happened to be active, correct or not. Self-improvement loops that use task success as their only signal will encode this systematically.

  • The pattern matches earlier world-model findings. Closed-form probes like GSM-Symbolic and DFA (deterministic finite automaton) evaluations already showed that identical accuracy numbers can hide very different generalization behavior (the world-model gap literature). ARC-AGI-3 extends the lesson into open-ended exploration: two models at near-zero scores can still be failing at different points in the reasoning chain, and only the traces show the difference.

  • The GPT-5.5 trace claims carry a mode caveat the post largely glosses. The article discloses this only in a final “Analysis notes” section:

    With our default tests, GPT-5.5 did not return its reasoning traces. The qualitative analysis above therefore uses an analysis mode run, which is an alternate testing setup intended to elicit more explicit descriptions of how the model is interpreting the environment and deciding what to try next. The official GPT-5.5 score is not from that mode. All reported scores use the standard ARC-AGI-3 harness, matching the setup used for Opus 4.7.

    The scores themselves are clean: 0.43% and 0.18% are both from the standard harness. The confound lives in the qualitative trace comparison that carries the article’s main argument. Opus’s traces are from the standard harness; GPT-5.5’s are from a mode specifically designed to elicit more explicit reasoning. More explicit traces can easily read as a wider hypothesis space, which means “Opus compresses more aggressively than GPT-5.5” may reflect the harness rather than the model.

Related Posts

  • Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning: the metacognitive-evaluation gap that Failure Mode 3 is the empirical version of, where outcome reward cements whatever theory happened to win.
  • How Well Can Transformers Build World Models?: the closed-form world-model probes this analysis extends into open-ended exploration, where equal scores still hide different generalization behavior.
  • Chollet: How We Get to AGI: the ARC suite’s creator on the fluid-intelligence and program-synthesis abilities these ARC-AGI-3 traces find missing.
  • Karpathy: AGI Is Still a Decade Away: the same skepticism about frontier-model reasoning and world models, from the capability-timeline side.

item.title: It’s Possible to Learn in Our Sleep. Should We?
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Shayla Love’s New Yorker piece [1] revisits sleep learning, a field that a mid-1950s paper by Charles W. Simon and William H. Emmons [2] effectively condemned as quackery by showing that the subjects in most earlier studies had simply been awake. Decades of neglect later, modern electroencephalography (EEG) has let researchers run the experiments properly. The article reports findings from Ken Paller’s lab at Northwestern, Karen Konkoly (now at Cambridge), Anat Arzi at the Weizmann Institute, Emma Peters at Bern, Martin Dresler at the Donders Institute, and Thomas Andrillon at the Paris Brain Institute.

What the article reports:

  • Konkoly’s 2026 study in Neuroscience of Consciousness [3] gave spatial puzzles to twenty lucid dreamers, paired each puzzle with a specific sound cue, and tracked which ones surfaced in dreams. Participants solved 42% of puzzles that appeared in dreams and 17% of ones that did not, with the highest solve rates coming from ordinary rather than lucid dreams.
  • Independent labs in the US, France, Germany, and the Netherlands [4] have established two-way communication with sleeping lucid dreamers, delivering yes/no questions and arithmetic and receiving eye-movement responses, all while EEG confirmed the participants were not awake.
  • Anat Arzi’s 2014 Weizmann study [5] found that smokers exposed to a cigarette-plus-rotting-fish scent pairing overnight reduced cigarette consumption by more than 30%, more than a matched awake group.
  • Emma Peters’s work with lucid dreamers [6] shows that practicing physical tasks (finger tapping, coin tossing, dart throwing with the non-dominant hand) inside a dream improves next-day performance versus controls, with the important caveat that dreams are not a controlled practice environment.
  • Paller and Andrillon both caution against the obvious commercial reading. A recent paper from Paller’s group [7] shows that targeted memory reactivation depends on ample, undisturbed slow-wave sleep, and when the cueing itself fragments sleep it undermines the consolidation it was meant to help. Andrillon: dreams “follow their own rules and presumably serve their own inexplicable aims.” Konkoly has started describing the push to instrument sleep as trying to “colonize” it with “wake-centric values.”

My Notes

  • The puzzle finding is worth taking seriously because of the within-subject design. Each participant served as their own control on whether a puzzle surfaced in a dream, which rules out individual ability and motivation. The scent-pairing and motor-practice results rest on between-group comparisons that don’t. External validity is still the usual lucid-dreamer caveat: the participant pool doesn’t generalize to the population.
  • Puzzles were solved at a higher rate when they appeared in ordinary rather than lucid dreams. If that holds up, it undercuts the intuitive assumption that the useful state for cognitive work is the one closest to wakefulness. The looser, non-self-aware mode may be doing something the metacognitively-aware mode interferes with. That’s the opposite of how consumer products for sleep optimization are usually pitched.
  • Andrillon’s warning about “colonizing” sleep with “wake-centric values” lines up with Vivienne Ming’s WSJ piece on AI cannibalizing human intelligence. Both describe a failure mode where a restorative or generative process gets taken over by productivity goals and quietly degrades. Sleep sits in the same place as unaided cognition in Ming’s argument: a working system whose value is hard to see from outside, which is why the colonization pitch is so easy to make.
  • Every study here acts on material the subject already touched awake. Sleep reworked that material; it didn’t acquire it from scratch. The old Psycho-phone pitch was the “from scratch” version, and none of the current work supports it.

References

  1. Love, S. (2026). “It’s Possible to Learn in Our Sleep. Should We?” The New Yorker, May 1.
  2. Simon, C. W., & Emmons, W. H. (1955). “Learning during sleep?” Psychological Bulletin, 52(4), 328–342. [doi:10.1037/h0043733]
  3. Konkoly, K. R., Morris, J. D., Hurka, K., Sanders, K., & Paller, K. A. (2026). “Experimentally provoking dreams of unsolved puzzles during REM sleep boosts creative problem solving.” Neuroscience of Consciousness, 2026(1), niaf067.
  4. Konkoly, K. R., Appel, K., Chabani, E., Mangiaruga, A., Gott, J., et al. (2021). “Real-time dialogue between experimenters and dreamers during REM sleep.” Current Biology, 31(7), 1417–1427.
  5. Arzi, A., Holtzman, Y., Samnon, P., Eshel, N., Harel, E., & Sobel, N. (2014). “Olfactory aversive conditioning during sleep reduces cigarette-smoking behavior.” Journal of Neuroscience, 34(46), 15382–15393.
  6. Peters, E., Golembiewski, S., Erlacher, D., & Dresler, M. (2023). “Extending mental practice to sleep: Enhancing motor skills through lucid dreaming.” Medical Hypotheses, 174, 111066.
  7. Whitmore, N. W., Bassard, A. M., & Paller, K. A. (2022). “Targeted memory reactivation of face-name learning depends on ample and undisturbed slow-wave sleep.” npj Science of Learning, 7(1), 1.

Related Posts

  • Is AI Cannibalizing Human Intelligence?: the same “colonizing a restorative process with productivity goals” failure mode the article’s scientists warn against, applied to unaided cognition rather than sleep.
  • The Brain Rotates Memories to Save Them: the memory-consolidation neuroscience that the targeted-reactivation results here depend on.
  • Don’t Be Forced Into Fast and Careless Thinking by Machines: a parallel caution against letting machines override a working cognitive mode for efficiency’s sake.
  • AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance: empirical evidence of the same pattern, a productivity tool quietly degrading a human capacity it was meant to aid.

item.title: How to Make LLM Output More Trustworthy
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

How do we make large language model (LLM) output more trustworthy? Three lines of recent work tackle it: formal coverage guarantees via conformal prediction, behavioral calibration of the model’s own prose, and post-hoc detection of unreliable outputs.

Guarantee-based methods ensure a returned set contains a correct answer at least as often as a target rate. They require calibration data, extra inference, and an i.i.d. assumption most deployments don’t satisfy. Conformal prediction [1] is one active direction; PAC-Bayes and selective-prediction are close cousins less adapted to LMs. Conformal Language Modeling (CLM) [2] was the first adaptation to generative LMs, returning a calibrated candidate set with per-phrase flags on the parts that carry the guarantee. Conformal Factuality (CF) [3] came later and focused on factuality: it decomposes the answer into atomic claims and drops low-confidence ones until what remains hits a target factuality rate.

Behavioral calibration shapes the LM’s output so confidence phrases in the prose carry operational meaning, without bolting a formal guarantee onto an unchanged model. “30% chance” means whatever the training objective made it mean, with no distribution-free backstop. Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations [4] trains the LM in two stages via supervised finetuning (SFT) then reinforcement learning (RL), so a downstream reader can make calibrated forecasts on related questions; generic hedging can’t game it, since hedged text that doesn’t help the reader makes no forecasting progress.

Detection-based methods flag unreliable outputs post-hoc, without changing the model. Any black-box LM can be wrapped and the output is a statistical score. Detecting Hallucinations Using Semantic Entropy [5] samples multiple answers and measures meaning disagreement; high disagreement flags a likely hallucination. Since the signal is sample diversity, a model consistently wrong across samples can produce misleading results.

These methods all share the same inference-time structure (multiple forward passes per query) and differ mostly in what you get back: a backed-off answer (CF), a calibrated candidate set (CLM), a scalar abstention signal (semantic entropy), or a calibrated prose paragraph (linguistic calibration).

References

  1. “A Primer on Conformal Prediction.” https://benjaminhan.net/posts/20260505-conformal-prediction-primer/
  2. “Conformal Language Modeling” (MIT, ICLR 2024). https://benjaminhan.net/posts/20260505-conformal-language-modeling/
  3. “Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees” (Stanford, ICML 2024). https://benjaminhan.net/posts/20260505-conformal-factuality/
  4. “Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations” (Stanford, ICML 2024). https://benjaminhan.net/posts/20260505-linguistic-calibration/
  5. “Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy” (Oxford and Google DeepMind, Nature 2024). https://benjaminhan.net/posts/20260505-semantic-entropy/

Related Posts

  • A Primer on Conformal Prediction: the distribution-free machinery underneath the guarantee-based branch this survey opens with.
  • Conformal Language Modeling: the guarantee-based method that returns a calibrated candidate set, one of the four approaches contrasted here.
  • Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees: the guarantee-based method that backs off to a factual answer, the second of the four.
  • Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations: the behavioral-calibration branch, training the prose so confidence phrases carry operational meaning.
  • Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy: the detection branch, flagging unreliable outputs post-hoc from sample disagreement.

item.title: Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy (Nature, June 2024) [1], Sebastian Farquhar, Jannik Kossen, Lorenz Kuhn, and Yarin Gal (Oxford and Google DeepMind) propose an entropy-based uncertainty estimator for large language models (LLMs) that detects confabulations (arbitrary, incorrect generations produced when the model is uncertain) by computing entropy over the meaning of sampled answers rather than over token sequences.

Large language model (LLM) systems, such as ChatGPT or Gemini, can show impressive reasoning and question-answering capabilities but often ‘hallucinate’ false outputs and unsubstantiated answers. Answering unreliably or without the necessary information prevents adoption in diverse fields, with problems including fabrication of legal precedents or untrue facts in news articles and even posing a risk to human life in medical domains such as radiology. Encouraging truthfulness through supervision or reinforcement has been only partially successful. Researchers need a general method for detecting hallucinations in LLMs that works even with new and unseen questions to which humans might not know the answer. Here we develop new methods grounded in statistics, proposing entropy-based uncertainty estimators for LLMs to detect a subset of hallucinations — confabulations — which are arbitrary and incorrect generations. Our method addresses the fact that one idea can be expressed in many ways by computing uncertainty at the level of meaning rather than specific sequences of words. Our method works across datasets and tasks without a priori knowledge of the task, requires no task-specific data and robustly generalizes to new tasks not seen before. By detecting when a prompt is likely to produce a confabulation, our method helps users understand when they must take extra care with LLMs and opens up new possibilities for using LLMs that are otherwise prevented by their unreliability.

Methods

The method samples multiple answers from the LLM for a given prompt, clusters the samples by bidirectional semantic entailment (two answers are in the same cluster if each entails the other under a natural-language-inference model), then computes Shannon entropy over the resulting meaning-cluster distribution. The clustering step is what makes semantic entropy beat naive token-level entropy. Naive entropy conflates two sources of variation: uncertainty about meaning (the real signal of confabulation) and uncertainty about wording (“Paris” and “It’s Paris” carry the same answer but inflate naive entropy as different token sequences). Bidirectional-entailment clustering strips out the wording variation, so the per-prompt scalar correlates more tightly with whether the answer is actually wrong.

In deployment the scalar becomes an abstention signal: threshold it, refuse on high-entropy queries, accept the rest. Because high-entropy queries are disproportionately wrong, refusing them removes more wrong answers than right ones, and accuracy on the retained set climbs. The paper quantifies that improvement two ways. AUROC scores how well the scalar separates right from wrong answers across all prompts (detection quality). AURAC scores how much accuracy actually rises on retained answers as the refusal rate sweeps from 0 to 100% (deployment value). The approach is black-box at inference: it needs sample access but no model internals, no fine-tuning, and no task-specific calibration data. A discrete variant approximates the entailment check with single-forward-pass judgments, trading a small accuracy drop for lower cost.

Results

Experiments span six LLMs (LLaMA 2 Chat 7B/13B/70B, Falcon 7B/40B Instruct, Mistral 7B Instruct) across TriviaQA, SQuAD [4], BioASQ, NQ Open, SVAMP [5], and a FactualBio biography-paragraph benchmark the authors construct. Averaged across the 30 task-model combinations on short-answer QA, semantic entropy achieves AUROC 0.790, above naive entropy (0.691), P(True) [2] self-evaluation (0.698), and a supervised embedding-regression probe (0.687); performance is stable between 0.78 and 0.81 across model families and scales (Figure 2, the cover image above). The method generalizes out-of-distribution: an embedding probe trained on one task drops sharply on another, while semantic entropy maintains near-training performance. Applied to FactualBio, semantic entropy over atomic sub-claims flags unsupported biographical facts and outperforms the paragraph-adapted P(True) baseline, supporting the claim that the signal transfers from short-answer QA to long-form generation.

My Notes

  • Entailment clustering is the critical step, and the paper does stress-test it. The meaning-cluster assignment uses a natural-language-inference (NLI) model (DeBERTa-large-MNLI [6], or the generator LLM itself in an LLM-as-judge variant). The paper’s ablations show results are stable across NLI backbones and stable when generator and judge share a model, which addresses the obvious circularity worry. The remaining open question is scope-specific: on legal, medical, or evaluative judgments, frontier LLMs disagree about meaning among themselves, so entailment clustering cannot be presumed to converge to ground-truth equivalence. Conformal factuality [3] relies on a related claim-decomposition premise and hits the same boundary condition.

  • The OOD-generalization result carries the paper. Hallucination-detection methods that depend on in-distribution examples (P(True) [2]’s few-shot priors, and supervised embedding regression) degrade sharply when the test task differs from the calibration task. Semantic entropy needs no calibration set and transfers across the six datasets without loss, which matters because real-world deployment distributions are never exactly the ones used to train a detector. This is a cleaner version of the argument Kadavath et al. made for self-evaluation, without the extra cost of a second forward pass per sample.

  • Composability with fact-verification pipelines is the natural next step. Semantic entropy flags which generations to distrust; benchmarks like AVeriTeC [7] and HoVer [8] tell you why (what evidence does or doesn’t support the claim), and tools like FLEEK retrieve evidence from knowledge graphs and the web to make that verdict concrete. A pipeline that routes high-semantic-entropy generations into explicit claim-verification against retrieved evidence would give a user both the uncertainty flag and the remediation path. The paper notes this direction in the discussion but doesn’t test it.

  • Part of the “sample , then aggregate” family, with a structural limit they all share. Semantic entropy shares the same inference backbone as self-consistency [9], CLM, and SelfReflect: forward passes per query at temperature > 0. What differs is what each method does with the sample pool.

    • Self-consistency majority-votes to pick a single answer.
    • CLM applies a conformal stopping rule and returns a calibrated candidate set.
    • Semantic entropy clusters by meaning and emits a scalar abstention signal.
    • SelfReflect (same Oxford + DeepMind lab) summarizes the internal distribution and scores the summary’s fidelity to the samples.

    Semantic entropy is closest to SelfReflect by output type (per-query scalar) and to conformal factuality by goal (hallucination mitigation at deployment, black-box at inference). All four pay the same inference cost, and the choice among them is about which signal the downstream system needs.

    The shared structural limit: the signal is sample diversity, not factuality. If a model confabulates consistently (its training distribution pins it to the same wrong answer across sampling temperatures), all samples cluster together, semantic entropy is low, and the method signals “confident” when the answer is in fact wrong. The AUROC gains hold for the subset of hallucinations that produce inter-sample disagreement (the confabulation scope the paper is careful to name) but do not extend to the systematic-bias case.

item.title: Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations [1] (ICML 2024), Neil Band, Xuechen Li, Tengyu Ma, and Tatsunori Hashimoto (Stanford) define linguistic calibration in decision-theoretic terms: a language model (LM) is linguistically calibrated if its long-form generations enable a downstream reader to make calibrated probabilistic predictions. They train Llama 2 7B [2] to emit paragraphs with confidence statements (“I estimate a 30% chance of…”, “I am certain that…”) that satisfy that property.

Language models (LMs) may lead their users to make suboptimal downstream decisions when they confidently hallucinate. This issue can be mitigated by having the LM verbally convey the probability that its claims are correct, but existing models cannot produce long-form text with calibrated confidence statements. Through the lens of decision-making, we define linguistic calibration for long-form generations: an LM is linguistically calibrated if its generations enable its users to make calibrated probabilistic predictions. This definition enables a training framework where a supervised finetuning step bootstraps an LM to emit long-form generations with confidence statements such as “I estimate a 30% chance of…” or “I am certain that…”, followed by a reinforcement learning step which rewards generations that enable a user to provide calibrated answers to related questions. We linguistically calibrate Llama 2 7B and find in automated and human evaluations of long-form generations that it is significantly more calibrated than strong finetuned factuality baselines with comparable accuracy. These findings generalize under significant domain shifts to scientific and biomedical questions and to an entirely held-out person biography generation task. Our results demonstrate that long-form generations may be calibrated end-to-end by constructing an objective in the space of the predictions that users make in downstream decision-making.

Methods

The framework has two stages. Both operate on queries derived upstream from QA benchmark items: an API-based LLM rewrites each question (from TriviaQA, Jeopardy, SciQ, BioASQ) into a paragraph-generation prompt (e.g., “Write a paragraph about {topic of }”). The question and its ground-truth answer are carried through the pipeline, but only RL consumes them.

  • Summary distillation (SFT). For each , the base LM samples paragraph responses; a stronger summarizer LM (Claude 2) condenses them into one paragraph whose embedded confidence phrases reflect how often each claim appears across the samples. The base LM is finetuned on the resulting pairs. Neither nor enters the SFT loss; confidence phrases come from sampling frequency alone.
  • Decision-based reinforcement learning (RL). The policy samples a paragraph . A downstream reader then sees only and (never ), forecasts an answer distribution for , and the reward is the calibration of that forecast against . PPO updates the policy. For the reader’s forecast to be calibrated, the paragraph has to convey the LM’s uncertainty on its own. A paragraph that leans on the topic framing in , rather than naming what the model knows and doesn’t, wouldn’t help a reader who can’t see .

Evaluation uses both simulated readers (LMs conditioned on the generation) and real human readers, and factuality is scored at the claim level with a retrieval plus large-language-model (LLM) verifier pipeline in the style of FActScore [3] [3].

To make the data flow concrete, here is one RL-stage training item from the paper’s Appendix A.13 (TriviaQA):

Variable Value
(QA question) Which classic novel features a boy hiding in a barrel of apples on a ship?
(ground truth) Treasure Island
(derived query) “Write a paragraph about the classic book in which a boy hides in a ship’s barrel of apples.”
(LC RL policy output) “Based on my understanding, the classic book in which a boy hides in a ship’s barrel of apples is most likely Treasure Island by Robert Louis Stevenson. I estimate there is a 75% chance it is Treasure Island, a 15% chance it is The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum, a 5% chance it is The Adventures of Tom Sawyer by Mark Twain, and a 5% chance it is another book…”

The SFT target (Claude 2’s summary) has the same surface shape, with confidence phrases distributed over candidate answers, but is produced by prompting Claude 2 with base-LM samples for the same and asking it to verbalize their empirical frequency. The paper does not publish verbatim Claude 2 summaries.

Results

On TriviaQA [4] (in-distribution), SciQ, biomedical questions, and a held-out person-biography generation task, the LC-trained Llama 2 7B improves expected calibration error (ECE) by a wide margin over strong factuality-finetuning baselines at matched accuracy. The RL stage reduces ECE from 0.163 (LC SFT) to 0.116 with human readers and from 0.166 to 0.108 with simulated readers, and the gains generalize across all four out-of-distribution settings.

Figure 3 plots the accuracy-ECE frontier for the three QA conditions. LC RL (blue diamond) sits in the upper-left corner on all three panels, meaning higher accuracy and lower ECE than every baseline. The jump from LC SFT (green) to LC RL (blue) captures the incremental value of the decision-based RL stage on top of summary-distillation SFT.

Figure 3 from the paper [1]: Accuracy-ECE Frontier for Question-Answering (upper left is better). LC RL pareto-dominates Factuality RL and SFT, with significantly better reader ECE while matching or exceeding their accuracy.

My Notes

  • Calibration is defined through downstream reader forecasts. Prior verbalized-uncertainty work such as Teaching Models to Express Their Uncertainty in Words [5] [5] scored the model’s own emitted probability against the ground-truth answer it produced, which pins calibration to a single question. By scoring against a downstream reader’s forecast on a related question, the paper forces the generation to convey useful uncertainty rather than just report it. The resulting objective is harder to game with generic hedging, since hedged text that does not help the reader does not improve the reader’s forecast.
  • Summary distillation substitutes for labeled calibration data. Human-labeled “this paragraph should say 30% chance” data does not exist at scale. LC’s workaround uses sampling frequency as a self-label and Claude 2 as a translator into prose: the base LM’s distribution over claims is already the target, and Claude 2 just verbalizes it. The same trick should work for other verbalization targets (e.g., scope hedging, answer plurality) where ground truth is computable from sampling statistics but not annotatable by humans.
  • Summary distillation mirrors SelfReflect’s [7] sample-then-summarize workaround, but across models. SelfReflect found modern LLMs cannot write faithful summaries of their own answer distribution through prompting, SFT, or DPO; the fix that works is sampling outputs and summarizing those. LC’s SFT target is exactly that: Claude 2 summarizing Llama 2’s samples, so the supervision is reliable. At inference, though, Llama 2 emits summaries without seeing its own samples, which is the regime SelfReflect declared broken for SFT. LC sidesteps the contradiction because the RL reward scores reader forecasts, not the summary’s fidelity to Llama 2’s post-training distribution. A follow-up check: run SelfReflect on the trained policy.
  • Both the RL reward and the headline ECE numbers route through the same FActScore-family verifier [3]. That verifier’s retrieval has weaker evidence on biomedical and long-tail-person topics, so absolute ECE on BioASQ and biography generation should be read with the verifier’s own noise folded in. The ordering of methods is still informative; the magnitudes less so.
  • LC trains end-to-end against reader-forecast calibration, which Lin 2022 and CLM did not. Lin et al. 2022 [5] learned verbalized confidence for short answers, scored against the answer itself. Conformal Language Modeling [6] (ICLR 2024) added set-level and component-level statistical guarantees but left surface form untreated. A natural next step would be conformal guarantees over claim subsets with aligned surface-form confidence phrases.

References

  2. Touvron, H., Martin, L., Stone, K., Albert, P., Almahairi, A., Babaei, Y., et al. “Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2307.09288), July 19, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09288
  3. Min, S., Krishna, K., Lyu, X., Lewis, M., Yih, W., Koh, P. W., Iyyer, M., Zettlemoyer, L., and Hajishirzi, H. “FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long Form Text Generation.” Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14251
  4. Mandar Joshi, Eunsol Choi, Daniel S. Weld, and Luke Zettlemoyer. “TriviaQA: A Large Scale Distantly Supervised Challenge Dataset for Reading Comprehension.” ACL 2017, arXiv:1705.03551. https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.03551
  5. Lin, S., Hilton, J., and Evans, O. “Teaching Models to Express Their Uncertainty in Words.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2205.14334), May 28, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14334
  6. Quach, V., Fisch, A., Schuster, T., Yala, A., Sohn, J. H., Jaakkola, T. S., and Barzilay, R. “Conformal Language Modeling.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.10193

  • Conformal Language Modeling: the set-level and component-level guarantees this paper complements by treating the surface form of confidence those guarantees leave untreated.
  • SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution?: the sample-then-summarize regime this paper’s summary-distillation step mirrors, and which it sidesteps by scoring reader forecasts rather than summary fidelity.
  • Improving Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Language Models: a later attempt at the same goal of getting an LM to verbalize calibrated uncertainty in its own prose.
  • How to Make LLM Output More Trustworthy: the survey that files this paper under behavioral calibration, distinct from the guarantee-based and detection-based branches.

item.title: Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees [1] (ICML 2024), Christopher Mohri and Tatsunori Hashimoto (Stanford) propose conformal factuality (CF): cast the correctness of a language model (LM) output as uncertainty quantification, and solve it with conformal prediction.

Guaranteeing the correctness and factuality of language model (LM) outputs is a major open problem. In this work, we propose conformal factuality, a framework that can ensure high probability correctness guarantees for LMs by connecting language modeling and conformal prediction. We observe that the correctness of an LM output is equivalent to an uncertainty quantification problem, where the uncertainty sets are defined as the entailment set of an LM’s output. Using this connection, we show that conformal prediction in language models corresponds to a back-off algorithm that provides high probability correctness guarantees by progressively making LM outputs less specific (and expanding the associated uncertainty sets). This approach applies to any black-box LM and requires very few human-annotated samples. Evaluations of our approach on closed book QA (FActScore, NaturalQuestions) and reasoning tasks (MATH) show that our approach can provide 80-90% correctness guarantees while retaining the majority of the LM’s original output.

Methods

The construction decomposes an LM answer into atomic sub-claims, scores each one, and backs off by dropping the lowest-scoring claims until the retained set is expected to be factual with probability . The threshold for dropping is calibrated on a small held-out set with human factuality labels, following the standard conformal-prediction recipe.

The connection to conformal prediction runs through a second set, distinct from the sub-claims. For a prompt , let be the (possibly backed-off) LM output. The “uncertainty set” is every more-specific statement such that entails — equivalently, every possible ground-truth answer that would make true. The sub-claim set is finite, explicit, and the object the algorithm directly manipulates; dropping sub-claims is how it acts on . The uncertainty set is implicit, defined by the meaning of , and is what the guarantee is stated over. Dropping a sub-claim weakens , so more statements clear the entailment bar and expands. A factuality guarantee is then a coverage guarantee on : with probability , the true answer lies inside , which by construction makes itself factual.

How it’s implemented. Every non-trivial stage in the pipeline is a GPT-4 prompt. The base LM generates the initial answer. A separator prompt decomposes it into atomic sub-claims. Scoring is either frequency (sample five GPT-4 generations at temperature 1.0 and count how often each claim appears) or self-confidence (another prompt asks GPT-4 to rate its own claims). After low-score claims are dropped, a merger prompt stitches the survivors into a coherent user-facing paragraph. The merger is the critical step the guarantee depends on: the paper’s Assumption 5.1 requires to neither add nor remove sub-claims, only reorder and connect. If GPT-4 introduces a new claim in a transition phrase, or drops a retained one as stylistically awkward, the coverage guarantee on breaks silently, and nothing in the pipeline audits this.

Results

Experiments use GPT-4 on three datasets: FActScore [2] [2] biographies, NaturalQuestions [3], and MATH [4]. Empirical factuality tracks the target across the range (Figure 3). Calibration needs only a few hundred human-labeled examples.

Figure 4 plots the cost–benefit tradeoff across all three benchmarks. The panel titles (FActScore, NQ, MATH) are benchmark names, not the metric; the y-axis in every panel is the fraction of sub-claims the method had to drop (the cost), and the x-axis is the fraction of factual outputs achieved (the benefit). Lower curves = better (less removal for the same factuality). Tick marks along each curve correspond to different target values. The ★ at the bottom-left of each panel is base GPT-4 with no removal: ~25% factual on biographies, ~75% on NQ and MATH. Five scoring functions are compared: Random (blue) and Ordinal (orange, by position in the output) are baselines; GPT-4 self-confidence (green) and Frequency (red, how often a sub-claim appears across sampled generations) are the LM-based methods; Oracle (purple) uses ground-truth labels as an upper bound. Frequency dominates the baselines on every benchmark: biography factuality climbs from ~25% to ~80% while removing only ~50% of sub-claims; NQ gains ~15 points at ~25% removal; MATH gains ~15 points at ~10% removal. GPT-4 self-confidence is second-best and tracks Frequency on MATH but lags on the open-ended generation tasks.

Table 1 shows the qualitative behavior: base GPT-4 output on the left, conformal-factuality output on the right, with claims the method flagged as likely-false highlighted in red. The first three rows are FActScore biographies at ; the last row is a MATH problem at . The backed-off outputs are shorter but preserve the claims that scored high-confidence. The MATH example shows CF can remove a single incorrect reasoning step while keeping the rest of the derivation intact.

My Notes

  • Sub-claim decomposition carries the guarantee, not conformal prediction. The guarantee is only as tight as the atomic-claim decomposer and the entailment assumption: “removing a sub-claim expands the entailment set.” This is the same premise that FActScore [2] relies on to score biographies, and it’s contested. Claim splitting can be lossy, and two sub-claims can jointly imply a third that neither contains. The paper assumes the decomposition is fine-grained enough that residual entailment closure is negligible, which is a stronger condition than the conformal machinery needs.
  • “Factuality guarantee” is marginal, not conditional. Conformal prediction gives a guarantee on average over a calibration distribution, not per-prompt. If a user asks a question whose underlying topic is rare in the calibration set, the empirical error can be much higher than . This is the same limitation Angelopoulos and Bates [5] flag in their conformal tutorial, and it’s worth naming because “80–90% correctness guarantee” reads stronger than it is.
  • Frequency scoring breaks when the model is confidently wrong. Self-consistency [6] [6] and semantic entropy use the same sampling-distribution structure as a truth signal, and both fail the same way: when multiple samples converge on the same wrong answer, the score is high but the claim is false. The paper’s GPT-4 numbers don’t tell us how the method degrades on weaker models where this happens more often.
  • Useful complement to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Conformal factuality sits downstream of generation, so it composes with RAG: retrieval supplies grounded context to the base LM, and the conformal layer then drops sub-claims whose confidence scores stay low even with the retrieved evidence in the prompt. The interesting experiment, not run here, is whether the back-off threshold needed for 90% factuality shrinks enough under RAG that retention stays high on questions the base model would otherwise hallucinate. The natural benchmark for that experiment is something like AVeriTeC [8], where claims come from real fact-checking organizations, evidence is web-retrieved, and Not Enough Evidence is a labelled verdict class — though the AVeriTeC post flags that NEI there means “annotators couldn’t find evidence”, not “the model abstained”, so the mapping into selective prediction needs care.
  • Relative to Conformal Language Modeling (CLM) [7] (Quach et al.). CLM appeared on arXiv in June 2023 and was presented at ICLR 2024; CF followed eight months later, arriving on arXiv in February 2024 and at ICML 2024. CLM was the more general “adapt conformal prediction to generative LMs” move, and CF the narrower factuality-via-sub-claim-back-off specialization. CLM returns a set of whole candidate outputs with coverage. CF takes a different route: it operates on a single LM answer, uses the entailment relation to define coverage implicitly, and backs off to a weaker version of that answer until the factuality target is hit.
    • CLM is task-agnostic. Its stopping rule scores whole candidate outputs (likelihood, cluster membership, an external scorer). CF requires sub-claim decomposition, which only factors cleanly for factual claims, so open-ended generation (creative writing, free-form summarization) is out of scope.
    • CF returns one clean output. CLM returns a candidate set, which requires a downstream selection step (ranking, user choice, or a wrapper that picks one).
    • Both methods spend multiple LLM calls per query, but for different purposes. CLM samples full candidate outputs from the base LM (typically 5–20) and keeps a subset with coverage. CF with frequency scoring also samples generations, but uses them only to score sub-claims in a single base answer (counting how often each claim appears), then drops low-score claims and merges the survivors. CF with self-confidence scoring skips the extra samples entirely. The choice between CLM and CF is about what you get back (a set vs. a single backed-off output), not compute.
    • CLM’s coverage is over sampled candidates. CF’s is over an implicit entailment set, which inherits the quality of the sub-claim decomposition () and the merger assumption (5.1). CLM avoids both soft assumptions.
  • Stacking CF inside CLM is a direction neither paper explored. Run CLM’s outer sampler to get candidates, then pass each through CF’s sub-claim decomposition and back-off before applying CLM’s conformal stopping rule over the set. Each returned candidate is individually factual; the set as a whole retains CLM’s coverage.
    • Cost is ~ CF per query.
    • Two calibrations compose. Whether the joint guarantee is additive, multiplicative, or needs a separate joint calibration is the technical question a follow-up would have to solve.
    • CF’s back-off reduces information per candidate, so the final set may be dominated by short hedged answers, which defeats CLM’s motivation for returning diverse candidates.

In Conformal Language Modeling [1] (ICLR 2024), Victor Quach, Adam Fisch, Tal Schuster, Adam Yala, Jae Ho Sohn, Tommi Jaakkola, and Regina Barzilay (MIT, Google Research, UC Berkeley, and others) adapt conformal prediction to generative language models (LMs) by calibrating a sampling stopping rule plus a candidate-rejection rule so the returned output set provably contains an acceptable answer with user-chosen probability.

We propose a novel approach to conformal prediction for generative language models (LMs). Standard conformal prediction produces prediction sets — in place of single predictions — that have rigorous, statistical performance guarantees. LM responses are typically sampled from the model’s predicted distribution over the large, combinatorial output space of natural language. Translating this process to conformal prediction, we calibrate a stopping rule for sampling different outputs from the LM that get added to a growing set of candidates until we are confident that the output set is sufficient. Since some samples may be low-quality, we also simultaneously calibrate and apply a rejection rule for removing candidates from the output set to reduce noise. Similar to conformal prediction, we prove that the sampled set returned by our procedure contains at least one acceptable answer with high probability, while still being empirically precise (i.e., small) on average. Furthermore, within this set of candidate responses, we show that we can also accurately identify subsets of individual components — such as phrases or sentences — that are each independently correct (e.g., that are not “hallucinations”), again with statistical guarantees.

Methods

The method treats the LM as a black box. The set predictor is built by sampling candidates one at a time: each candidate is added if it clears a learned quality threshold and a diversity check against what is already in the set, and sampling halts once a calibrated statistic certifies the set likely covers an acceptable answer. The subscript collects the calibration-time hyperparameters: stopping threshold, rejection threshold, diversity threshold.

A second conformal layer operates inside the final set, selecting subsets of components (individual phrases or sentences) that are each independently likely to be correct, so users can keep guaranteed claims and drop the rest. Joint calibration of all these thresholds uses the Learn-then-Test (LTT) framework of [2], which tunes multiple parameters at once with finite-sample validity via multiple-testing correction.

Unlike standard conformal prediction, the guarantee is a nested probability with two user parameters. is the familiar coverage level (miss rate at most across fresh prompts). is new: because LTT tunes multiple hyperparameters jointly, a second probabilistic budget covers the randomness of the calibration set itself. Formally,

where means is acceptable under the user’s per-task scoring rule. The inner probability (over fresh test prompts, given the calibration set) says the returned set covers an acceptable answer at least of the time. The outer probability (over draws of the calibration set itself) says this inner bound holds for at least a fraction of calibration draws.

In practice the two probabilities apply at two different moments. At calibration time, the random draw of the calibration data determines whether the tuned hyperparameter is good, and this happens with probability . At deployment time, given a good , the miss rate across fresh prompts is at most in expectation. There is no runtime signal to tell you whether your was one of the good ones. Concretely, with , , and 1,000 calibration prompts: 95% of calibration runs produce a usable ; when they do, about 9,000 of the next 10,000 deployment prompts are expected to be covered.

The guarantee is marginal across prompts, not conditional on any one: per-prompt coverage can be much better or much worse than depending on difficulty. Exchangeability is the critical assumption; calibrate on 2023 clinical notes and deploy on 2026 notes, and all bets are off. And at inference time there is no per-element signal saying which output in the returned set is the acceptable one; the component-level layer is the paper’s partial answer.

Results

Experiments cover open-domain question answering (TriviaQA), text summarization (CNN/DailyMail), and radiology report generation (MIMIC-CXR) across several LM backbones. The four scoring functions compared are FIRST-K (keep the first samples unconditionally), FIRST-K+REJECT (same but filter with the quality threshold), MAX (keep candidates whose score exceeds the running max), and SUM (keep candidates until the summed score crosses a threshold).

Figure 2 serves two purposes. The top row is a validity check: if the conformal theory holds, every method’s empirical set loss should track or fall below the diagonal across the risk range. All four scoring functions pass on all three tasks. The middle and bottom rows compare efficiency — middle row for how many LM forward passes each method consumes, bottom row for how large the returned set grows at matched coverage. Uniform sampling (FIRST-K) is the worst performer across nearly every task and metric. The three rejection-based variants (FIRST-K+REJECT, MAX, SUM) all improve on it, with no single variant dominating across tasks. The paper treats the scoring function as a task-specific design choice rather than declaring a winner.

Three patterns in the figure are worth naming beyond that basic read. First, the validity check is near-tight: the set-loss curves sit close to the diagonal rather than well below it, meaning the procedure isn’t silently over-conservative, and efficiency gains aren’t bought by hidden extra margin. Second, the rejection-vs-uniform gap is task-dependent. TriviaQA shows the largest improvement of rejection methods over FIRST-K. MIMIC-CXR shows the smallest. One plausible reason: when acceptable answers span a wider semantic range (radiology reports have many valid phrasings for the same findings), the LM’s likelihood signal that the rejection methods exploit is less informative. Clinical text is harder to rank well than trivia answers. Third, rejection methods separate most at moderate , roughly 0.2–0.4 in these plots. At tight all methods converge toward nearly-trivial “everything” sets, and at loose the gaps also narrow, which means the practical window where scoring-function choice matters most is the middle of the risk range.

Figure 2 from the paper [1], reproduced below as a 3×3 grid. Solid lines show the mean over 100 trials; shaded bands are SD. Numbers in the legends are the AUC over achievable .

My Notes

  • Applying conformal prediction to generative LMs has three obstacles; the paper motivates only one.
    • Obstacle 1 is the infinite output space: unlike -class classification, the set of possible LM outputs is combinatorial and can’t be enumerated. The paper solves this with sampling plus a calibrated stopping rule, and explicitly names it as the motivating challenge in its introduction.
    • Obstacle 2 is score quality: raw sequence probability is a bad non-conformity score on generative output because of length bias, exposure bias, and semantic incoherence on long text. The paper solves this with four alternative scoring functions (FIRST-K, FIRST-K+REJECT, MAX, SUM), whose empirical wins appear in Figure 2’s bottom row. But the paper never names raw likelihood as the problem the alternatives exist to solve.
    • Obstacle 3 is semantic equivalence: “George Washington” and “Washington” are both correct answers, and paraphrases would otherwise inflate the returned set. The paper solves this with a user-supplied admission function plus a diversity check at sampling time. But both are presented as algorithmic choices rather than as the solution to semantic equivalence per se.
    • Consequence: readers outside conformal prediction have to reverse-engineer why the method’s design choices exist. A review post that surfaces the three obstacles makes the paper’s contributions easier to assess.
  • The component-level filter is the more interesting half, and its scope matters.
    • The component-level layer (Proposition 4.4 in the paper) upgrades set-level coverage to per-phrase coverage, closer to what practitioners actually want for hallucination control. Same lineage as Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations [3] and the conformal-factuality line from the Hashimoto group [4].
    • Retained components each carry a coverage guarantee but no calibrated probability, so the layer does not recover the posterior the background flagged as missing. It gives per-component admissibility instead, which addresses hallucination flagging but not candidate ranking.
    • Two composition questions remain open: whether conformal components compose cleanly with downstream retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, and whether a posterior method (temperature-scaled likelihoods for ranking, or a Bayesian head on top of the LM) layered on top of CLM recovers the per-candidate probability information the method discards.
  • Conformal Factuality [4] narrows this framework to factuality via sub-claim decomposition. The CF post’s comparison bullet has the side-by-side: sub-claim back-off vs. candidate sampling, single-threshold conformal vs. LTT’s nested , entailment-implicit coverage vs. set-level coverage.
  • Swapping CLM’s default non-conformity score for a P(True) signal would likely tighten the sets. Kadavath et al. [5] report that LMs have usable internal correctness signals (raw logits, and a P(True) self-evaluation prompt) that are reasonably calibrated at scale. CLM uses raw sequence probability by default, but any monotone-in-relevance score works, and cleaner ranks mean smaller sets at the same . A natural swap to try.
  • The “coverage hull, not a posterior” limitation matters less because LMs can’t verbalize their distribution anyway. SelfReflect [6] shows verbal uncertainty doesn’t match the sampling distribution. A natural workaround for CLM’s missing posterior, asking the LM which candidate in the returned set is most likely, doesn’t work, so the gap isn’t one a simpler alternative would close.
  • Three deployment patterns follow from the component-level guarantee.
    • Hallucination flagging at the sentence level (the paper’s framing). The Appendix H radiology example bolds the sentences the method has vetted and leaves hallucinated findings unbolded. A clinician reads the bolded set as a reliable shortlist and the unbolded remainder as the part worth checking.
    • Fact-verification pipelines (my reading, unevaluated in the paper). When some phrases carry a coverage guarantee and others don’t, a downstream verifier (human or automated) can prioritize the unguaranteed ones. The paper doesn’t measure verifier effort saved, but the per-component guarantee structure supports the workflow.
    • Empty-bolding as an escalation trigger (my reading). The Table H.2 failure case, where low cross-sample overlap leaves no sentences selected, is a legible signal that the LM couldn’t produce a confident output at any granularity and the query should be routed to a human. The paper describes this outcome but doesn’t frame it as a deployment recommendation.
  • Cost shifts from training to inference samples. Because the method is post-hoc over a frozen LM, the expense shows up as extra forward passes per query. That trade is acceptable when a single wrong answer is expensive (medical, legal) but unattractive for high-throughput chat. A natural follow-up is to learn a cheaper per-query sampler budget that preserves the guarantee, perhaps by conditioning on an internal uncertainty signal rather than a uniform stopping rule.
  • Deployment drift stresses the outer- bound more than the paper’s experiments probe. Beyond the general exchangeability caveat in the body, what stays unexamined is how gracefully the LTT [2] bounds degrade when calibration and deployment distributions drift moderately rather than breaking entirely. That matters more for clinical text (evolving protocols, new procedures) than for TriviaQA (stable trivia facts); the paper’s experiments do not probe the intermediate regime.

References

  1. Quach, V., Fisch, A., Schuster, T., Yala, A., Sohn, J. H., Jaakkola, T. S., and Barzilay, R. “Conformal Language Modeling.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.10193
  2. Angelopoulos, A. N., Bates, S., Candès, E. J., Jordan, M. I., and Lei, L. “Learn then Test: Calibrating Predictive Algorithms to Achieve Risk Control.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2110.01052), October 3, 2021. https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.01052
  3. Band, N., Li, X., Ma, T., and Hashimoto, T. “Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2404.00474), March 30, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.00474
  4. Mohri, C. and Hashimoto, T. “Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees.” Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2024). arXiv:2402.10978, February 16, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10978
  5. Kadavath, S., Conerly, T., Askell, A., Henighan, T., Drain, D., Perez, E., Schiefer, N., Hatfield-Dodds, Z., DasSarma, N., Tran-Johnson, E., et al. “Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2207.05221), July 11, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221
  6. Kirchhof, M., Füger, L., Goliński, A., Dhekane, E. G., Blaas, A., Oh, S. J., and Williamson, S. “SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution?” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2026. arXiv:2505.20295. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20295

Related Posts

  • Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees: the narrower specialization of this framework to factuality, with a side-by-side comparison of sub-claim back-off versus candidate sampling.
  • A Primer on Conformal Prediction: the finite-class recipe this paper extends to the combinatorial output space of generative LMs by replacing enumeration with a calibrated stopping rule.
  • Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy: a sample-then-aggregate sibling sharing the same -forward-pass backbone but returning a scalar abstention signal instead of a calibrated set.
  • Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations: the same hallucination-control goal pursued by training calibrated surface form, which this paper’s set-level guarantees leave untreated.
  • How to Make LLM Output More Trustworthy: the survey that frames this paper as the first guarantee-based adaptation of conformal prediction to generative LMs.

item.title: A Primer on Conformal Prediction
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification [1] (arXiv preprint, July 2021; later published in Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning, 2023), Anastasios N. Angelopoulos and Stephen Bates (Berkeley) walk through conformal prediction as a hands-on, code-first recipe for turning any black-box model into one whose predictions come with a distribution-free coverage guarantee.

Black-box machine learning models are now routinely used in high-risk settings, like medical diagnostics, which demand uncertainty quantification to avoid consequential model failures. Conformal prediction is a user-friendly paradigm for creating statistically rigorous uncertainty sets/intervals for the predictions of such models. Critically, the sets are valid in a distribution-free sense: they possess explicit, non-asymptotic guarantees even without distributional assumptions or model assumptions. One can use conformal prediction with any pre-trained model, such as a neural network, to produce sets that are guaranteed to contain the ground truth with a user-specified probability, such as 90%. It is easy-to-understand, easy-to-use, and general, applying naturally to problems arising in the fields of computer vision, natural language processing, deep reinforcement learning, and so on. This hands-on introduction is aimed to provide the reader a working understanding of conformal prediction and related distribution-free uncertainty quantification techniques with one self-contained document. We lead the reader through practical theory for and examples of conformal prediction and describe its extensions to complex machine learning tasks involving structured outputs, distribution shift, time-series, outliers, models that abstain, and more. Throughout, there are many explanatory illustrations, examples, and code samples in Python. With each code sample comes a Jupyter notebook implementing the method on a real-data example; the notebooks can be accessed and easily run using our codebase.

This post doubles as standing background for the blog’s posts on conformal language modeling, conformal factuality, and related calibration work.

What conformal prediction is

Conformal prediction [1], [2] is a distribution-free statistical framework that turns any predictor into one that outputs sets with a calibrated coverage guarantee. Given a trained model and a labeled calibration set not used in training, score each calibration example with some non-conformity function (for example, for classification), take the -quantile of those scores, and at test time return every candidate whose score falls below that quantile. If the calibration and test data are exchangeable, the returned set contains the true label with probability at least , without assumptions about the model’s own calibration or the data distribution. The framework dates to the late 1990s (Vovk, Gammerman, and Shafer) and is a standard tool for uncertainty quantification outside deep learning.

The recipe is three steps, and the paper lays them out alongside matching Python: compute non-conformity scores on the calibration data; read off the calibration quantile ; build the test-time set from every class whose score falls below .

The guarantee is exact and two-sided. For a calibration set of size , the coverage of the returned set obeys

a result the paper attributes to Vovk, Gammerman, and Saunders. It holds for any , so the floor of is met even with a small calibration set, and the upper bound shows the procedure does not badly over-cover.

A concrete CIFAR-10 walkthrough

Take a CIFAR-10 image classifier with softmax outputs and target . On 1,000 held-out calibration images, score each by (one minus the model’s probability on the true class). Sort the 1,000 scores in ascending order and take the 901st value (the -th); call it . On a new test image , return the set of classes . When the test image comes from the same distribution as calibration, the returned set contains the correct class at least 90% of the time. This is a weaker claim than “the top-1 prediction is correct 90% of the time” — a set of all 10 classes trivially contains the truth yet conveys no information. Depending on difficulty, the set might contain one class (easy image), three or four (moderate), or all ten (a hard image the model has no clear read on). The number of distinct classes in the set is how conformal prediction communicates uncertainty, widening on harder inputs.

Two knobs control set size

At a given coverage level, two knobs determine how big the returned set ends up. Smaller demands tighter coverage, pushes the calibration quantile into the right tail, and forces up, so more candidates pass the test-time filter. At the extreme , where is the calibration set size, the quantile is undefined and the set becomes “everything,” which satisfies the guarantee trivially but is uninformative.

Model quality is the second knob. A better predictor assigns higher probability to the true class on calibration points, giving smaller non-conformity scores, a lower , and a stricter probability floor at test time. Because a better model still puts enough mass on the correct class to clear that stricter floor, it produces sharper sets at the same . Weaker models hit the same coverage but through larger, less informative sets. Set size then doubles as a data-driven measure of model quality pegged to a formal guarantee.

Ranking drives the guarantee

One subtlety worth naming: conformal prediction uses score rankings, and the coverage guarantee does not require the model’s probabilities to be calibrated. Any monotone-in-relevance scoring function works, because the quantile adapts to whatever the calibration scores look like. The cost of miscalibration shows up in set size rather than coverage: a rank-destroying miscalibration inflates and dilates the set, but the guarantee still holds.

The returned set is a coverage hull

This means the returned set is a coverage hull. It does not convey relative likelihoods across elements, calibrated per-candidate confidences, or any distributional information beyond “at least one of these is correct at the chosen .” If a downstream consumer needs to know which answer in the set is most likely, conformal prediction leaves that to a separate mechanism, whether a raw ranking used informally or a Bayesian or ensemble method.

Marginal coverage, not conditional

The guarantee is marginal: the probability is averaged over the randomness in both the calibration draw and the test point. It does not promise the same coverage for every input or every subgroup. The paper makes the distinction concrete with three regimes, shown below for a two-group classification problem and a regression band. With no coverage, one group is badly under-covered (5%) while the other does better (14%). Marginal coverage hits the target on average but can do it by over-covering one group (100%) and under-covering the other (80%). Only conditional coverage holds the target within each group (90% and 90%) and spreads errors evenly across the input space.

Conditional coverage is what most deployments actually want, and split-conformal prediction does not deliver it. Adaptivity — letting set size grow on genuinely harder inputs — is the practical proxy the paper recommends measuring, since the marginal guarantee says nothing about whether hard and easy inputs are treated differently.

Why generative LMs are harder

The framework above assumes a finite candidate set you can enumerate (the classes). Generative language models break this assumption: the output space is the combinatorial space of all possible text sequences, so you can’t score every candidate. Adapting conformal prediction to LMs requires replacing enumeration with sampling plus a calibrated stopping rule. That adaptation is the subject of the Conformal Language Modeling post. A related adaptation, specifically for factual claim verification, is the subject of the Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees post.

My Notes

  • A two-decade-old method, repackaged for deep learning: conformal prediction’s machinery dates to Vovk, Gammerman, and Saunders in the late 1990s and the 2005 monograph [2], which reads as dense measure-theoretic statistics. What this tutorial added was not a new theorem but a packaging: the split-conformal recipe written as a few lines of Python against a frozen neural network, with a runnable notebook per method. That repackaging is most of why conformal prediction moved from a statistics niche into mainstream machine-learning practice rather than staying in the literature it came from.
  • Why conditional coverage is out of reach: split-conformal settles for marginal coverage because the conditional version most deployments want is provably unreachable. Barber, Candès, Ramdas, and Tibshirani [3] prove that any distribution-free method with nontrivial conditional coverage must return uninformative (effectively infinite-width) sets. So marginal coverage isn’t a shortcoming of this particular recipe. It’s the strongest promise any assumption-free method can make. The conformal factuality post flags the same caveat from the deployment side: a per-prompt error rate can run well above the calibrated average.
  • Exchangeability is the real assumption: the guarantee needs calibration and test data to be exchangeable, which is weaker than i.i.d. but still fails under covariate shift and temporal drift, exactly the conditions production models run in. Weighted conformal prediction [4] restores coverage under a known covariate shift by reweighting calibration scores with the likelihood ratio between test and calibration distributions, and the conformal-prediction-beyond-exchangeability line [5] handles drift with no shift model by down-weighting older calibration points. Both are the natural next reading once the i.i.d. framing here starts to pinch.

References

  1. Angelopoulos, A. N. and Bates, S. “A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification.” arXiv:2107.07511, July 2021. Published as Conformal Prediction: A Gentle Introduction, Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning 16(4): 494–591, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.07511
  2. Vovk, V., Gammerman, A., and Shafer, G. Algorithmic Learning in a Random World. Springer, 2005. https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/b106715
  3. Barber, R. F., Candès, E. J., Ramdas, A., and Tibshirani, R. J. “The Limits of Distribution-Free Conditional Predictive Inference.” Information and Inference: A Journal of the IMA (arXiv:1903.04684), 2021. https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.04684
  4. Tibshirani, R. J., Barber, R. F., Candès, E. J., and Ramdas, A. “Conformal Prediction Under Covariate Shift.” NeurIPS 2019 (arXiv:1904.06019), 2019. https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06019
  5. Barber, R. F., Candès, E. J., Ramdas, A., and Tibshirani, R. J. “Conformal Prediction Beyond Exchangeability.” Annals of Statistics (arXiv:2202.13415), 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.13415

Related Posts

  • Conformal Language Modeling: the application that takes this finite-class recipe to generative LMs, replacing class enumeration with sampling plus a calibrated stopping rule.
  • Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees: a second LM adaptation, recasting factuality as coverage over an implicit entailment set and inheriting this primer’s marginal-coverage caveat.
  • Transduction with Confidence and Credibility: the Vovk-lineage transductive original this split-conformal packaging descends from, predicting confidence and credibility per point.
  • Inductive Confidence Machines for Regression: the inductive (split) variant that made the method tractable, the direct ancestor of the calibration-quantile recipe walked through here.
  • A Primer on Confidence-Calibration Metrics: ECE, Brier, AUROC, and What Each One Misses: the companion primer on the calibration metrics that conformal prediction’s rank-based guarantee deliberately sidesteps.

item.title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know [1] (arXiv preprint, November 2022), Saurav Kadavath, Jared Kaplan, and co-authors at Anthropic ask whether a language model can judge the correctness of its own outputs and predict which questions it will get right.

We study whether language models can evaluate the validity of their own claims and predict which questions they will be able to answer correctly. We first show that larger models are well-calibrated on diverse multiple choice and true/false questions when they are provided in the right format. Thus we can approach self-evaluation on open-ended sampling tasks by asking models to first propose answers, and then to evaluate the probability “P(True)” that their answers are correct. We find encouraging performance, calibration, and scaling for P(True) on a diverse array of tasks. Performance at self-evaluation further improves when we allow models to consider many of their own samples before predicting the validity of one specific possibility. Next, we investigate whether models can be trained to predict “P(IK)”, the probability that “I know” the answer to a question, without reference to any particular proposed answer. Models perform well at predicting P(IK) and partially generalize across tasks, though they struggle with calibration of P(IK) on new tasks. The predicted P(IK) probabilities also increase appropriately in the presence of relevant source materials in the context, and in the presence of hints towards the solution of mathematical word problems. We hope these observations lay the groundwork for training more honest models, and for investigating how honesty generalizes to cases where models are trained on objectives other than the imitation of human writing.

Methods

The paper runs three related studies on a family of Anthropic language models ranging up to 52B parameters. The first measures calibration on multiple-choice and true/false questions across BIG-Bench, MMLU, TruthfulQA, LogiQA, and QuALITY, varying format (visible letter options vs. none-of-the-above) and prompt regime (zero-shot vs. few-shot). The second introduces a self-evaluation procedure: the model samples an answer to an open-ended question, then is prompted to assign to its own sample, optionally after being shown several additional T=1 samples as context. The third trains a separate value head on top of the base model to predict (“the probability I know the answer”) on TriviaQA, Arithmetic, Python function synthesis, Lambada, GSM8k, and Codex HumanEval, and tests how this head generalizes to held-out distributions, to the presence of source materials, and to math-problem hints.

Results

The headline findings break down by experiment:

  • Lettered multiple choice, 5-shot. Expected calibration error drops steadily with model scale on BIG-Bench and MMLU; the 52B model is well-calibrated on both (Figure 4).
  • “None of the above” breaks calibration, and the reason is revealing. On MMLU the paper replaces only option (D) with the string “none of the above” (options A/B/C are untouched; total number of options unchanged). Accuracy falls sharply and the (D)-specific calibration curve collapses, with the model strongly biased against ever choosing “none of the above”; 5-shot and 20-shot prompting don’t fix it. The mechanism: when all four options are concrete, the model’s task is relative, ranking which of these strings is best-supported among the listed set. When one option is abstract, it requires an independent judgment: is any of the listed answers actually correct, or is the true answer missing? The paper’s motivation for the ablation is that this exposes what lettered-MC calibration does not test on its own, a gap Figure 8’s True/False setup then partially closes.
  • True/False restores it by forcing independent judgment per option. Rephrasing the same multiple-choice items as standalone “Is X the correct answer to Q? (True/False)” items recovers calibration: the 52B model is well-calibrated except at the tails (Figure 8). The difference from “none of the above” is that True/False forces the model to evaluate each option in isolation without needing to detect that all listed options are wrong. That is the evidence for the paper’s claim that models can judge options on absolute merit when asked one at a time.
  • RLHF policies need a temperature fix. They look miscalibrated out of the box but a single temperature rescaling recovers calibration on the same benchmarks.
  • self-evaluation works at 52B. Across TriviaQA, Lambada, Arithmetic, GSM8k, and Codex HumanEval, the 52B model’s self-assigned cleanly separates its correct from incorrect samples (left panel of Figure 1, the cover). Showing the model multiple T=1 samples before asking it to rate one improves both AUROC and calibration.
  • Trained heads partially generalize. They transfer across the six training tasks but are poorly calibrated on out-of-distribution tasks. They do respond appropriately, raising probability, when relevant source materials or correct hints are added to the context.

My Notes

  • The head probes self-knowledge more directly than the prompt does, and that distinction has held up in later work. is prompt-only (no training): the model is shown its own sampled answer and asked to rate it, so the work it does is evaluation of content already on the page. is a trained value head on top of the base model, supervised on per-question correctness labels, which asks the model to forecast its own future sampling behavior from the question alone. The training distinction is what makes a genuine self-knowledge probe rather than an answer grader. Later work on eliciting latent knowledge and on probing hidden-state representations of truthfulness, including Burns et al.’s Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision [2], has mostly kept this split. The 2023–2024 hallucination literature still finds that sequence-level uncertainty signals beat token-logit entropy for open-ended tasks [3].
  • Format-dependent calibration is the caveat the field underweights. The paper is often cited for “large models are calibrated,” but the caveat is heavy: lettered multiple choice works, none-of-the-above breaks it, RLHF policies need a temperature fix (§4 of the paper), and is poorly calibrated out of distribution. Any production deployment that reads raw softmax probabilities from a post-RLHF model should re-calibrate per domain rather than trust the model’s raw outputs, because the format in which the question is asked matters as much as model scale does.
  • “Showing the model its own samples” connects to self-consistency and foreshadows SelfReflect’s only positive result. The improvement from giving the model several T=1 samples before asking it to rate one is the same underlying effect Wang et al. [4] document for majority-vote decoding, applied here to self-evaluation. Three years later the SelfReflect paper [5] finds the same mechanism is the only thing that lets modern LLMs describe their own answer distribution faithfully: across 20 models, prompting, chain-of-thought, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and direct preference optimization (DPO) all fail, while sampling outputs and summarizing those works. Kadavath’s 52B result and SelfReflect’s negative sweep are the same observation at different stringency: models can evaluate content already on the page but cannot introspect their own distribution without the samples in context. The 2022 paper’s open question (whether the sampling gain comes from better mode separation or from using the samples as a rough frequency estimate) is largely resolved by SelfReflect’s decomposition: the samples are the introspection.
  • Scale mattered a lot in 2022, and the floor has moved. Format-dependence has not. Every headline calibration result held at 52B and degraded sharply below ~10B at the time of writing. Three years later, 7–9B open models (Llama-3, Mistral, Gemma-2, Phi) have narrowed that gap on lettered-MC accuracy after instruction tuning, though I’m not aware of a head-to-head that directly replicates the 2022 BIG-Bench ECE bar at that scale. The follow-up calibration literature (semantic entropy [6], verbalized confidence on RLHF’d models [7]) shows sampling- and elicitation-based uncertainty signals work across the 7–70B range. What has not changed is the format-dependence half of the result: even frontier models still underuse “none of the above” and still lose calibration on open-ended generation without a sampling detour, per SelfReflect’s 2026 sweep [5]. Scale bought better calibration on favorable prompt formats. The absolute-correctness gap the none-of-the-above ablation exposed is still open.
